text.p: The following are some of the leading stories in Finnish papers this morning.
HELSINGIN SANOMAT
- Opposition growing against second Finance Minister Arja Alho's model for subsidising household services.
- Wheelchairs among the weapons of physically disabled women learning self-defence on course.
- Ministry of interior affairs plans new ways to make municipal mergers more attractive.
- Finland's poorest suffered the most from recession.
- Relations between the Paper Workers Union and the Federation of Finnish Forest Industries are tightening in the aftermath of wildcat strikes last week.
- Parliament arguing about pension fund administration in connection with a larger reform.
- Finnish techno music is moving into St Petersburg via the underground community.
KAUPPALEHTI

- The Government Guarantee Fund's (GGF), Suomen Vakuutus Oy's and German Hermes Kredit Versicherungs AG's joint credit insurer for small and medium size companies due to start up this spring, GGF managing director says.

- Nokia research centre to move to new premises in Helsinki's Ruoholahti in 1999. Swedish rival Ericsson to build a sales and marketing building near Nokia's new headquarters in Tapiola in Espoo, just outside Helsinki.
- Finnish MEPs questioning European Commission about its decision not to allow Finland's tax exemption on sweetener Xylitol .
- Employers' social costs and the value-added-tax are the biggest barriers to employment, says researcher at the small and medium-sized companies' lobby.
HUFVUDSTADSBLADET
- Russian drivers on Finnish roads 10 times more likely to have accidents than Finns and locals in eastern Finland have learned to stay away from roads in Russian rush hours, police says.
- Parliament traffic committee demands that the traffic ministry ends the "slaughter" of postal services.
AAMULEHTI
- Finland's spending on education still among the highest in the OECD countries, OECD indicators show.
- President Martti Ahtisaari's South American tour to start on Sunday is a significant opening to diversify Finland's foreign policy and business.
-- Helsinki Newsroom +358-9-680 50 242
